content: Each uploaded file is associated with a dedicated image page. This concept also applies to other file types, such as sound files. For example, a sound file might be named Image:Schubert-Impromptu B-flat1.ogg. For an actual image, the image page typically displays the full-resolution image, although a reduced version may be shown depending on user preferences. In such cases, a link labeled Download high resolution version (x KB) is provided to access the full version. The image page also serves as a description page, offering detailed information about the image. If a project family has a Commons project, files are generally uploaded to Commons. The image page on Commons includes copyright information. When using internal image syntax (e.g., `[[Image:filename]]`), the filename is assumed to refer to a file within the same project if it exists there. Otherwise, it defaults to the file on Commons. When naming a file on Commons, avoid using a name already in use on any project where the file might be utilized unless the new file is intended to replace the local one (which would then be deleted) or if the Commons file is meant to be replaced locally without altering the links. An image hosted on Commons can have a separate image page on each project that does not already have a conflicting image with the same name. If the projects are language-specific, the local image page can include information about the image in the local language. This also allows the image to be categorized within the local category system and displays the local pages that use the image. To determine which pages across various projects use an image from Commons, it is essential to link the Commons image page to all corresponding local image pages. Even if a local image page has not been explicitly created and remains empty, linking to it will generate a page with an image links section that lists the local pages embedding the image. The interlanguage link feature is functional on Commons, enabling links to various language-specific Wikipedias. Links to other projects are displayed within the page. For example, commons:Image:Blank Go board.png links to the local image description page, which, due to the contents of `MediaWiki:Sharedupload`, is connected to the Commons page where the image was uploaded. Local content examples include Meta-Wiki, English, and Italian. Note that links from local content to Commons do not lead to a real image. To create a link to the description page of a sound file or an image without embedding the actual file, use a link like `[[:Image:filename]]`. For images, the leading colon prevents the image from being embedded in the article, creating a standard hyperlink instead. For sound files, autoplay is not possible, so the link functions similarly. The description page for an image or sound file consists of four main components: 1. The image itself (or the sound file, if applicable). 2. A description of the image or sound. 3. The Image history, which is analogous to the page history. 4. The Image links or File links section, which lists pages embedding the image or linking to the file using the Media: prefix. However, this section has limitations: It does not list links to the image page itself. For images embedded in templates, it lists only the template, not the pages where the template is used. To find those pages, use the What links here feature for the template. If an image in a template depends on a parameter containing the full image code, the image URL, or variables like `{{PAGENAME}}` or `{{PAGENAMEE}}`, neither the final page nor the template is listed. If only the caption is parameterized, the template is listed. Rare cases, such as uploaded HTML files linking to the image, are not included. For an image hosted on Commons, the local image page typically displays the following: The image itself. A message from `MediaWiki:Sharedupload`. Local editable content. The rendering of editable content from Commons, including transcluded content from other Commons pages. Note that sections are unnumbered and excluded from the table of contents, category tags are ignored, and internal links within Commons are styled as internal links but redirect to Commons. Variables dependent on the site refer to Commons. Additionally, the local pages using the image are listed. The description section of the page has its own edit history, labeled Image:xxx Revision history. This should not be confused with the Image history, which pertains to the file itself. The description section is particularly relevant for images. For sound files, additional guidance can be found in Wikipedia:Media. In the description section, you can include text. Initially, this section automatically contains the upload summary provided by the user during the first upload. This text also appears in the Image history section for the first upload entry. The description should provide details about the image, such as Image of a goldfish in a small tank. This description is not meant to serve as alternative text but rather as a temporary substitute for a proper `longdesc` tag. You may also include the image's dimensions in pixels. If other versions of the image exist, especially larger versions, links to them should be included. Text-free versions are particularly useful for multilingual usage. Categorizing Images Images can be categorized similarly to other pages but are treated separately. On category pages, images are not included in the article count and are displayed in a distinct section with thumbnails and filenames. On Commons, categories primarily consist of images. In projects with articles, categories may either mix articles and images on the same subject or separate them into distinct image categories. An image category is typically a subcategory of the general category for the subject and a subcategory of a broader image category. To categorize a new image, you do not need to edit the image page directly; you can simply add the category tag in the upload summary. Many images can be categorized under subcategories of Category:Images by subject. You may need to explore the category hierarchy to find the appropriate category. Nonexistent Images If an image does not exist, its page will not display an Image history section. For example, Image:Stop sign us.JPG demonstrates this. Editing When editing an image page, the preview only shows the editable portion, not the image itself, the image history, or the image links. The image file itself cannot be edited through this page; uploading a new file is required to replace the existing one. Protection Protecting an image page also protects the image file. This means that only a system administrator (sysop) can upload a new image under the same filename as the protected image.
